adu.strength_rationale: All four benchmark features are in West Virginia law for its cities, towns and villages: one ADU per lot by right, attached or detached, at least 600 square feet where the house has 800 square feet or more, with no added parking. Conflicting local rules become invalid on January 1, 2027, so the law counts for 80% of 2026 to 2030, and incorporated places hold 36% of the state's detached homes: 0.80 × 0.355 = 0.28 of the benchmark is in law. Homes outside cities and towns would be newly covered.
adu.notes: Changed from Adam: section numbers 8-40 to 8-42 (redesignated per the bill history 'Code Affected' list and the code site); size differs to supported_with_limits (75%/1,000 rule, same as Arizona's decision 92 reading); in_effect_from 2027-01-01 per the brief (act effective 2026-06-04, conflicting rules invalid 2027-01-01). Feature share 4 x 0.8001 / 4 = 0.80; coverage pending (municipalities only). Doubt worth a reviewer's eye: 8-42-1(a) defines an ADU as a unit that 'complies with ... any applicable regulatory requirements', which 8-42-1(d)(2)(C) says include 'Applicable zoning ordinances and conditions', and 8-42-3(e)(1) says the article does not 'Supersede applicable regulatory requirements'; read literally this could let local zoning narrow the mandate. Chapter 241 and approval date 3/14/2026 from the bill history page: https://www.wvlegislature.gov/Bill_Status/bills_history.cfm?input=659&year=2026&sessiontype=RS&btype=bill ; enrolled text: https://www.wvlegislature.gov/Bill_Status/bills_text.cfm?billdoc=sb659+sub1+enr.htm&i=659&sesstype=RS&yr=2026

entries.title: Baseline range, forecasts made in 2016 to 2020
entries.outcome: five-year building permit totals that fell inside the baseline range
entries.unit: runs inside, of 255; the range promises at least 80% (204)
entries.result_text: 251 of 255 five-year totals fell inside the range, against the 80% it promises; 3 were above it and 1 below.
entries.independence: The range's two numbers were fitted on forecasts made in 1990 to 2015; these later forecasts were never used in the fit. Their outcomes were already published, so this is a historical holdout, not a blind one.
entries.supports: The range holds the size of a typical five-year surprise in recent years.
entries.does_not_support: That the range will hold through a turn in the market (see the 2005-2010 row), or anything about the reforms.
entries.next_check: The 2026 permit totals, frozen before they are published.

entries.title: Baseline range, forecasts made in the 2005 to 2010 bust
entries.outcome: five-year building permit totals that fell inside the baseline range
entries.unit: runs inside, of 306; the range promises at least 80% (245)
entries.result_text: Only 56% of the forecasts made in the bust held the real total; 125 of the 134 misses were below the range, because a range fitted on history does not foresee a collapse.
entries.independence: These forecasts are inside the period the range was fitted on, so this measures how coverage moves with the market, not an out-of-sample test.
entries.supports: A plain warning shown beside every baseline: in a downturn the real total can fall below the range.
entries.does_not_support: A probability that 2026-2030 lands inside the range.
entries.next_check: Watch the 2026 totals against the range.

entries.title: Baseline range, forecasts made in the 2011 to 2015 recovery
entries.outcome: five-year building permit totals that fell inside the baseline range
entries.unit: runs inside, of 255; the range promises at least 80% (204)
entries.result_text: 75% of the forecasts made in the recovery held the real total, just short of the promise; 63 of the 65 misses were above the range.
entries.independence: In the fitting period; shown for how coverage moves with the market.
entries.supports: The range errs in both directions when the market turns.
entries.does_not_support: A probability for the forecast period.

entries.title: Baseline range refitted each year with only the data available then
entries.outcome: five-year building permit totals inside a range refitted each year on closed windows only

entries.independence: Each year's range uses only five-year windows that had closed by then.
entries.supports: A sober reading of the headline range: it describes past surprises, and a forecaster without hindsight would have been surprised more often.

entries.title: The 20-year swing range (Adam Ruege's rule), side by side
entries.outcome: five-year permit totals inside the slowest-to-fastest range of each state's prior 20 years
entries.result_text: Reproduced exactly from Adam's design: 181 of 255 inside, 37 above, 37 below. It promises no fixed coverage, so it is shown beside the headline range rather than scored against a promise.
entries.independence: A second way to draw the range on the same history.
entries.supports: The trade-off between a wide range that rarely misses and a tight one that follows each state's own swings.
entries.does_not_support: Choosing between them on one test window.
entries.credit: Rule designed by Adam Ruege (Housing Reform Estimator v2.0); his counts reproduced in this repository.
